summary: Introduces some Forward Error Correction (FEC) schemes that supplement RFC 3452. They use a more compact FEC Payload ID for reliable bulk delivery of large objects, and can send blocks of an object of indeterminate length in sequence. It is experimental and has been replaced by RFC 5445.

plainLanguage.summary: When you send puzzle pieces, some get lost. Extra spare pieces let the receiver rebuild the picture without asking again. This describes shorter labels for the pieces. RFC 5445 replaced it.

questions: what is forward error correction in bulk delivery
how does compact fec reduce overhead
subtitle: Forward error correction schemes with smaller packet headers for reliable bulk delivery.

tldr.problem: Forward error correction headers must carry information about which encoding symbol each packet contains, and some FEC schemes use large headers even when the sender can communicate block metadata out-of-band.
tldr.mechanism: Compact FEC defines two new FEC Encoding IDs—0 for no-code FEC (purely for interoperability testing) and 130 for compact FEC with actual encoding—both using a 32-bit payload ID instead of larger formats, with source block information communicated out-of-band.
tldr.outcome: Reduces packet header overhead while supporting both reliable bulk delivery of known-size objects and streaming delivery of blocks of indeterminate length. It is experimental and was replaced by RFC 5445.

today: RFC 3695 is Experimental and has been superseded by RFC 5445. It was designed as a building block for efficient FEC in reliable multicast.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3695 defines two new Forward Error Correction schemes, FEC Encoding IDs 0 and 130, that supplement the FEC Building Block (RFC 3452). These schemes are designed to reduce packet header overhead compared to FEC Encoding IDs 128 and 129 when the sender is able to transmit object metadata out-of-band before the data stream begins.

The key insight is that when all source blocks of an object have the same length, the receiver does not need the source block length in every packet header—it can be communicated once in the Session Description. This allows the FEC Payload ID to be half as long (32 bits instead of 64 bits), saving space in every packet.
sections.plainLanguage: If you know ahead of time that all puzzle pieces are 1000 bytes, you only need to write that once, not on every piece of paper. Compact FEC uses short labels because the big information is already known.

sections.title: FEC Payload ID Format
sections.content:
Both Compact FEC Encoding IDs 0 and 130 use the same 32-bit FEC Payload ID format, consisting of a 16-bit Source Block Number and a 16-bit Encoding Symbol ID.

The Source Block Number identifies which source block of the object the packet's encoding symbol came from. In unique SBN mode, consecutive blocks use Source Block Numbers 0 through 2^16 - 1, allowing up to 65,536 source blocks per object. In non-unique SBN mode, the same SBN may identify different blocks at different times, with the mapping communicated out-of-band.

The Encoding Symbol ID identifies which specific encoding symbol from the source block is in the packet payload. For FEC Encoding ID 0 (no-code), each symbol is simply consecutive bytes of the block. For FEC Encoding ID 130 (under-specified FEC), the symbol structure depends on the FEC Instance ID and algorithm chosen.
sections.plainLanguage: The 32-bit label is split in half: one half says which block (0, 1, 2...), the other half says which piece of that block (first part, second part, third part...).

sections.title: Compact No-Code and Compact FEC Schemes
sections.content:
FEC Encoding ID 0 (Compact No-Code) is a fully-specified scheme that performs no actual FEC encoding. Each encoding symbol consists of consecutive bytes from a source block. If a source block is X bytes and each symbol is L bytes, the block is partitioned into ceil(X/L) symbols, numbered 0 through N-1. The receiver collects these symbols in order to reconstruct the block. This scheme is primarily for testing interoperability between different FEC implementations, since no decoding is needed.

FEC Encoding ID 130 (Compact FEC) is an under-specified scheme where a non-trivial FEC encoding algorithm may be used. The FEC Instance ID specifies which algorithm to use. Like the no-code scheme, the source block and encoding symbol length are communicated out-of-band, and the receiver accumulates symbols until it can decode the block.

Both schemes support two delivery models: reliable bulk delivery of objects with known length (where the object length and number of blocks are communicated in advance), and block-stream delivery where blocks of indeterminate length arrive sequentially.
sections.plainLanguage: No-Code just cuts the data into pieces and sends them; if you get them all, you're done. Compact FEC does the same but optionally scrambles the pieces so you can recover even if some are lost, all with short labels.

sections.title: Delivery Models and Examples
sections.content:
For reliable bulk data delivery, the sender partitions a known-size object into equal-length source blocks, communicates the block size out-of-band, and sends encoding symbols using unique Source Block Numbers. If L = 1 KB per symbol and each source block is up to 2^16 * L = 65 MB, an object can be larger than a terabyte by using many blocks.

For block-stream delivery, the sender generates blocks of indeterminate length on the fly (e.g., live video frames encoded into blocks as they arrive) and sends packets for one block before moving to the next. Receivers reconstruct blocks sequentially, and acknowledgement may be block-based rather than byte-based. This supports applications from live streaming without feedback to ACK-based reliable block delivery.

In non-unique SBN mode for block streams, the sender can reuse Source Block Numbers after 2^16 blocks have been sent, reducing the time between reuse to allow delayed block reception validation.
sections.plainLanguage: Bulk delivery: you know the file is 10 GB, so you split it into 100 chunks and send pieces of each. Stream delivery: data arrives one chunk at a time (like live video) and you encode and send it piece by piece.

sections.title: Status and Interoperability
sections.content:
RFC 3695 is experimental, following RFC 2357 requirements for reliable multicast protocols. It was designed as a building block (RFC 3048) for protocol instantiations such as ALC (RFC 3450). The document itself registers FEC Encoding IDs 0 and 130 in the IANA FEC encoding namespace, and establishes a registry for FEC Instance IDs under Encoding ID 130.

This RFC has been superseded by RFC 5445, which refines the FEC schemes further. The primary value of Compact FEC schemes is reducing header overhead in systems that can communicate metadata out-of-band.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an experimental building block that was later improved. It's useful when you can tell receivers the block size beforehand, so you don't waste header space repeating it.

fields.name: Encoding Symbol ID
fields.desc: Identifies which encoding symbol from the source block is in the payload.
